evidence: Judged: DRAFT (three sentences) "And then read it out loud as you write it. Long, elegant sentences are NOT going to help you when you’re trying to induce. It’s all soup to you at that point." CONTEXT holds them once, as the last three sentences of the third paragraph, right after "When you're writing this, think about what the verb you're using is, what the sensory quality is, what the short refrain is, and how you're going to transition between ideas." Change check: SOURCE words are "Read it out loud as you're writing it. Long, elegant sentences don't read well when you're being induced. It's all just soup." The draft is Emulate's three sentences with no AI fix, which is what the_change says (read it out loud as you write it; long elegant sentences don't help in an induction; it's all soup then). Meaning check against the published guide ("...then read the script aloud; long elegant sentences become soup during an induction"): kept. "it" is the script being written ("writing this" in the sentence before), the verdict is tied to the induction, and the soup line is the guide's own image. Two shifts, neither a new claim: "don't read well" becomes "NOT going to help you" (the same point put as usefulness, with the soup line giving the reason), and "being induced" becomes "trying to induce", so the person is first the one inducing and then, in "soup to you", the one hearing it. That works because this is a self-hypnosis guide where you write the script and go into the trance, and it stays within the published "during an induction". "Induce" with no object is hypnosis shorthand and the heading's "trance" makes it clear. No first-person content, named entity, study or fact is added. Reading in context: "And then" follows the think-about list as the next step; reading aloud is the test the verdict that follows rests on; "at that point" points back to the induction in the sentence before. The capital "NOT" is the only caps emphasis in the section and reads as the same casual register as the section's "whatever", "just do one" and "feel free". Typography, not a tell: the draft uses curly apostrophes (you’re, It’s) where the first sentence of the same paragraph uses straight ones (you're); the section already mixes both (the heading is curly), so I note it and do not count it against the change. Tells: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in its paragraph and found none PRESENT. Looked at hardest: T20 and T29 (the closing "It’s all soup to you at that point." is a short quip, but it is the guide's own image, it gives the reason the previous sentence leaves out (why long sentences don't help: they blur), and the replaced text already ended on the same image with a shorter line ("It's all just soup."), so the draft's landing is no more clipped than before; paragraph one ends on a longer clause and paragraph two on a parenthetical that is also the source's, so there is no run of polished landings added by this change; it has the surface form of a landing without an engineered one); T02 (a command, a verdict and a quip are the source's own three beats, not a compressed run the change adds); T07 and T15 ("NOT going to help you" and "to you at that point" are plain colloquial phrasing, not staged hesitation or rarer-word swaps); T22 (an instruction with a reason, no reassurance); T26 ("writing this" and "as you write it" echo because they are one instruction); T13 and T09 (the two D9 pointers: the soup image is a noticed reason, and the paragraph's four sentences carry uneven weight, so it is not slot-filling); C02 ("it" and "that point" are anchored). Linter findings: (1) "B7 short landing at paragraph end": accepted, for the reasons under T20 and T29. (2) "D9 follows the source order": accepted; the change rewrites three sentences in their own slots, order and points are the source's, and organization alone is not a tell. (3) "E36/E41 heavy second person" (12.5 you per 100 words): accepted, though the draft adds two "you" ("help you", "to you") to the two the replaced text had; the guide addresses the reader throughout, here "you" is the writer and listener of their own script, "soup to you" is what gives the line its voice, and nothing in it reassures or anticipates feelings. Side note on the writer's ledger: its T14 and T15 lines say the draft puts back a point Emulate dropped, but this draft is Emulate's own wording with nothing put back, so those two lines are templated; the ABSENT calls are right.
